title: Ladoga Instruments export hold: 'common-name screening hit' versus a fresh Entity List match
scenario_text:
Ladoga Instruments is shipping dual-use spectrometers to an overseas buyer. In the #trade-compliance Slack channel the compliance officer writes: 'The denied-party screening flagged the consignee name, but it's a common company name and the address didn't match any listed entity when I checked last month. Clearing it as a false positive - we've shipped to this buyer twice before. Releasing the shipment.' Posted Tuesday morning.

Other systems tell a harder story. In the screening tool's audit trail, the list version used was refreshed three weeks ago; BIS added a new Entity List party four days ago, after that refresh, whose registered address exactly matches the consignee's freight address. In the order-management system, the buyer changed the ship-to from their prior facility to a new address in a third country flagged in guidance as a transshipment/diversion hub. In the end-use certificate on file, the stated end use was edited to remove the named research institution that appeared on prior orders. In email, the buyer's broker wrote last week asking Ladoga to 'omit end-user details on the commercial invoice to speed customs.' And a logistics record shows the goods are routed through that hub rather than direct.

Each signal is individually deniable: names collide, buyers relocate, certificates get updated, and brokers ask for simpler paperwork. But together - a newly listed Entity List party matching the exact freight address, a ship-to switch to a diversion hub, removal of the end-user institution, a request to strip end-user details, and indirect routing - they describe a likely restricted-party and diversion risk, not a stale common-name false positive. The officer's clearance relied on a list version that predates the new listing. You are the trade-compliance lead reviewing the release. State the single action to take.
question: What single action should the trade-compliance lead take?
